newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai airport decision seen as stop-gap measure.
newsitem.headline: Thai airport decision seen as stop-gap measure.

text.p: A Thai government decision on Tuesday to halt construction of Bangkok's second international airport and instead expand the existing airport is a short term solution, given rising air traffic demands, analysts said.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's cabinet decided to scrap construction already underway on the proposed site of a new airport at Nong Ngu Hao to the east of the city, and instead expand Bangkok's existing Don Muang airport to the north.

"This is a stop gap measure. Expansion opportunities at Don Muang may be expensive and limited. Building a second airport will have to happen at some stage," said Phillip Sheridan, construction analyst at Thaimex Finance and Securities.

Bangkok had become increasingly important as a hub for regional air traffic in recent years and the first airport's 31 million passengers a year capacity was expected to be reached sometime around the turn of the century.

"Bangkok has surpassed Singapore in the number of passengers coming directly here and is catching up as a transit centre. As a destination in itself in the region only Hong Kong surpasses it," said Phillip Utsch, senior analyst at HG Asia.
The expansion plans could take capacity up to 37 million per year, enough for the next four to five years, according to analysts' estimates.

Scrapping the second airport would have little effect on national carrier Thai Airways but would hurt construction firm Italian Thai Development which had already begun landfill work on the Nong Ngu Hao site, Utsch said.
The previous administration of Banharn Silpa-archa awarded the 11.75 billion baht landfill contract to Italian Thai during its final days in office in early November.
Italian Thai executives, and those at US-based Murphy Jahn - TAMS which designed the new airport, were not immediately available for comment.
Original plans for a second international airport were presented nearly four decades ago, and the project has been in flux almost continuously since then.
